assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstrations of record stability and accuracy, moved timekeeping into the 10^-18 regime. This is the kind of measurement advance I value most: it opens new observables (gravitational redshift over millimetres, searches for varying constants, dark-matter probes, relativistic geodesy) and underpins a coming redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made early demonstrations. Ye's group drove strontium clocks to the precision frontier, with the associated spectroscopy and many-body physics. The two-name configuration is clean; other groups (for example Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom) may be argued, but the decisive concept and flagship performance are credited to these two.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg) and compared across continents with fibre links. The results are mature and the field is stable. Timing is good, with the redefinition of the second still pending to add practical impact.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier recognition of laser precision spectroscopy and the frequency comb could be argued by some members as incremental.
Whether credit should extend to other groups developing lattice clocks is not settled by the supplied text.
Detailed priority claims are from my memory and not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene produced correlated insulators and superconductivity in a clean, tunable carbon system and started the field of twistronics and moire quantum materials. Theory predicted flat bands at a specific angle, and experiments realized and measured them. The impact on condensed matter has been broad and rapid, with many follow-on platforms.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 continuum-model flat-band prediction. Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the decisive 2018 experiments on correlated insulators and superconductivity. Eva Y. Andrei's earlier STM evidence of flat-band signatures is a real part of the story, and omitting her is a fairness concern. A three-person prize combining experiment and theory is plausible.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups, with extensive follow-up in several moire systems. The mechanism of superconductivity is still debated, so the interpretation is not fully settled, but the central discovery of correlated phases is robust. Possibly early by traditional Nobel standards, though the field is very active.
uncertainties: Origin of the superconductivity remains contested.
Credit for Andrei and for the co-authors of the 2018 papers, and dependence on sample quality, is unresolved.
Possible overlap with fractional Chern insulator work in other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single defect spins, mostly NV centres in diamond, give room-temperature nanoscale sensing of magnetic fields, temperature and electric fields, with uses in condensed matter, biology and quantum networks. As an experimentalist I see this as a clear case of a new measurement technique enabling observations that were not available before.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and colleagues demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins in 1997. Awschalom showed coherent control and generality across defect systems. Lukin contributed nanoscale sensing and quantum register experiments and concepts. Walsworth, and others outside the credited list such as Hanson and Jelezko, also have claims, so a three-person choice is a judgement call and the field is broad.
assessment.maturity: Single-spin detection is long confirmed and widely repeated. Sensing applications are increasingly mature, with commercial instruments. Recognition is timely, though the impact beyond physics is still developing.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over many groups, so a fair three-person split is difficult.
The balance between unique discovery and technique development is debatable.
Lukin's name also appears in a Rydberg-array candidate, which could affect committee balance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter waves for precision inertial sensing, gravimetry, measurements of G and the fine-structure constant, equivalence-principle tests and gravitational-wave detector concepts. It is a natural continuation of laser cooling and precision spectroscopy and has produced field-deployable instruments. The measurement physics is original and consequential.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group made early atom-beam interferometers with material gratings. Bordé introduced the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer and the theory of atomic phase shifts. Kasevich built light-pulse inertial sensors with record sensitivity. Three names are plausible, though others such as Chu, Keith and Mlynek also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups confirm the techniques, and precision results are stable. Some of the most ambitious goals (large-scale tests, gravitational-wave detection) are still ahead, so recognition may be somewhat early for the full impact.
uncertainties: Credit distribution among Pritchard, Bordé, Kasevich and others is not settled.
Whether this is best viewed as a discovery or as technology development under the prize criteria.
Potential perceived overlap with earlier prizes on laser cooling.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices were developed into controllable quantum simulators of Hubbard models, with the Mott insulator transition, single-site imaging and engineered gauge fields. The theoretical proposal combined with the experimental realisations established a new way of testing many-body theory by measuring clean model systems.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) gave the theoretical blueprint for the Bose-Hubbard model in lattices. Greiner and Bloch demonstrated the superfluid-to-Mott transition in 2002 and developed quantum gas microscopes. Esslinger's fermionic work and Cirac's role are other possible credits. The configuration is contested, with five credited names.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are reproduced widely and the field is mature. The open issue is how much new physics, versus simulation capability, has been delivered, since many key results reproduce known models rather than solve open problems.
uncertainties: Credit among five names, and overlap with the Rydberg and trapped-ion candidates that share Zoller and Cirac.
Impact on solving open condensed-matter problems is still limited by temperature and system size.
Zoller appearing in several candidates is a configuration problem for the whole prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade, proposed for quantum gates and demonstrated with single atoms, has led to programmable neutral-atom arrays, entangling gates and analogue simulation of spin models with hundreds of atoms. The platform is rising fast and the experimental control is impressive.
assessment.attribution: Lukin and Zoller proposed and drove blockade gates and arrays. Browaeys and Saffman demonstrated blockade between individual atoms. Saffman's role is substantive and his omission from a three-person set is a possible unfairness; Lukin, Browaeys and Zoller is a reasonable choice from the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Core blockade physics is confirmed across several groups, but the platform is evolving and error-corrected computation claims are recent. Probably early compared with more established measurement advances.
uncertainties: The platform is still maturing and fault-tolerance demonstrations are recent.
Allocation among Saffman, Browaeys, Lukin, Zoller and others is unresolved.
Possible overlap with other quantum-information candidates in a single prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling of microwave photons to superconducting artificial atoms practical, giving the readout and control architecture for superconducting qubits. It is a significant enabling step for leading quantum-computing hardware and for quantum optics on a chip, with coherence times improved by orders of magnitude.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf and others wrote the 2004 proposal; Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling. Steven Girvin is not in the credited list, which weakens the fairness of the theoretical credit. The two experimentalists plus Blais is a reasonable configuration from the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by independent groups and widely used. Because recent recognition may have gone to related superconducting-circuit physics, some members may see it as too close to a recent prize, though I cannot verify prize details from here.
uncertainties: Closeness to recent recognition of superconducting circuits may reduce room for this candidate.
Absence of Steven Girvin from the credited names limits attribution fairness.
Application impact is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The qPlus sensor with CO-functionalised tips brought atomic force microscopy to sub-molecular resolution, imaging bond order and charge distribution in single molecules and allowing on-surface chemistry to be observed directly. It is an instrument and method advance, which I weigh seriously, though scanning-probe microscopy was already recognised in 1986.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl designed the qPlus sensor; Gross and Meyer at IBM Zurich demonstrated CO-tip imaging in 2009. Credit looks reasonably clear and the three-name set is a natural fit, though earlier AFM pioneers are outside this discovery.
assessment.maturity: The technique is reproduced widely and used in surface science and molecular chemistry. It is mature, but its fundamental physics impact is narrower than the other candidates, and some would regard it as chemistry.
uncertainties: Whether the work is judged to be physics or chemistry.
Incrementalism relative to the earlier scanning-probe prize.
Reach beyond specialist surface-science communities is limited.
